newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovaks wait for result after chaotic referendum.
newsitem.headline: Slovaks wait for result after chaotic referendum.

text.p: Slovaks are waiting for the results of a referendum but a low turnout could make the vote invalid and many critics have already denounced it as a failed test of the former communist country's conversion to democracy.
Many thousands of voters refused to take part because of a dispute over the ballots, which asked them only about joining NATO.

A separate proposal on presidential elections had been deleted at the last minute in a feud between President Michal Kovac, who wants future presidents elected directly, and Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar, who might inherit presidential powers if the choice remains with parliament.
The Slovak Statistical Bureau said it finished processing the results early on Sunday and would present them to the Central Referendum Committee later today.
"It will be 2 p.m. at the earliest," a referendum press official said.
The referendum needs a turnout of more than 50 percent to be valid and TASR news agency said no more than 15 percent voted in many areas.
Opposition leaders, and a senior presidential official, met on Sunday to consider their reponse.
Government and opposition leaders on Saturday traded blame, and threats of legal action, over the chaos in a process which foreign diplomats had billed in advance as a test of democratic credentials.
"The referendum was thwarted by the government and Premier Meciar," opposition Christian Democratic Movement leader Ivan Simko told a joint opposition news conference on Saturday.
But parliament chairman Ivan Gasparovic, a Meciar follower, blamed Kovac and the opposition.
"The president also contributed to the failure of the referendum," he told Slovak television on Saturday. "He indirectly called on the population to boycott the referendum before it was held."
The government had tried to have the question on direct presidential elections declared illegal.
Kovac, who had called on voters to support both NATO membership and direct presidential elections, refused to vote and urged others to do the same.
"After this, it's out of the question that Slovakia will be invited to join NATO in the first round of enlargement," he said on Friday.
The dispute over presidential elections springs from a clause in the constitution requiring a three-fifths majority in parliament to elect the president.
If no candidate can muster a sufficient margin, as seems likely on the present strengths of the parties, presidential powers would pass to the prime minister.
